items.title: Sheila Jordan — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: I met these two young guys―Skeeter Spight and Leroy Mitchell... I said, “I‟d love to sing with you... They said, “Yeah, we‟ll help you... we became like the Lambert, Hendricks and Ross of that time... I started scatting with them... I remember Skeeter and, and Leroy... the two guys I sang with

ctx.x: Were your neighborhoods integrated or segregated?

We… you know what? At the time, I think they were segregated. But, but I found a way, you know, I found a way to find out where these guys were playing, where this music was happening „cause I knew it had to be happening. So uh, and I did. I found the Club Sudan, which was a place that a white couple from Canada… „Cause Canadians, believe it or… well, you probably know this already. They weren‟t into the same kind of prejudice that they were in the U.S. And uh, this couple had this club down there called the Club…

come to town, they‟d get us up to sing. And Bird, you know, and John Lewis. He‟d come with… I think he was with Diz one time. I can‟t remember, but he came one time―John Lewis. And uh, so I started, you know, trying to write lyrics like they did, you know, but I wasn‟t not near as good as they were. But I learned how to… and I didn‟t scat with them very much. I sorta just listened but I‟d sing the line with them, and then sometimes I would sing the lyrics and I learned a lot from those guys. And eventually, when…

items.title: Sheila Jordan interviewed by Monk Rowe, Middleburgh, New York, May 11, 2002
items.q: Skeeter Speight and LeRoy Mitchell... took me under their wing when I was very young... And they taught me a lot.

ctx.x: Yeah. You couldn’t get it out fast enough.
No, no. Not on “Confirmation,” or any of those tunes. So if I’m going to sing “Confirmation,” [scats] I mean I can’t do it. So I just learned in order — and plus I © Fillius Jazz Archive -5-

should also say that I had two wonderful young musicians that were wonderful singers in Detroit, Skeeter Speight and LeRoy Mitchell, we called him Mitch but his real name was LeRoy Mitchell. And those two guys took me under their wing when I was very young. They were young too but they were two young Afro-American musician singers, and I just wanted to do this music so bad. And the only thing was I was young and I drank a lot. And they’d say well we’ll teach you this, but you’ve got to stop drinking. And I did…

items.title: Sheila Jordan — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Skeeter and Mitch said, “Hey, Jeannie”... So they said, “Why don’t you go over during the break and sing... I said, “I told you those lyrics weren’t any good,” to Skeeter, you know, and Mitch.

ctx.x: And when you rehearsed, was it a cappella or did you have [inaudible/overlapping]?

Oh, yeah, no, it was a cappella. We‟d, you know, we‟d go over to a different home like their homes or… Oh, I think Mitch was a little older because he, he got married. So we would go to his house, Skeeter and I, I think. But that was years, you know… We were together quite a while, quite a few years. I mean, not… maybe like four or five, six years, I think. I‟m not sure. I can‟t remember. [laughs] Senior moment. But uh, but we, uh, we would get together and they‟d say, “This is how it goes.” „Course, I had…
Now if we go back to when you first heard Charlie Parker, what made it so distinctive or different than the music you had been listening to? What was it that captivated you about Charlie Parker?
